title: Object Pronouns and Reflexives
bigQuestion: How does Spanish say who does what to whom without repeating every noun?

story.title: Exam Day, 6:40 a.m.
story.kicker: Daniela has a chemistry final at 8:00, and everything that can go wrong does.
paragraphs: Daniela's alarm rings at 6:00. She turns it off and thinks, "Cinco minutos más" (five more minutes). At 6:40 her little brother shakes her shoulder. "¡Despiértate! ¡Es tarde!" (Wake up! It's late!) She sits up fast. Her chemistry final starts at 8:00, and the bus leaves at 7:15.

She runs to the bathroom. "Me ducho en tres minutos," (I shower in three minutes) she promises herself. She showers, brushes her teeth, and gets dressed: *me ducho, me cepillo los dientes, me visto*. Every one of those verbs has a little word in front of it: me. In Spanish, when you do something to yourself, the verb says so.

In the kitchen her mother holds out a folder. "Tus apuntes. No los olvides." (Your notes. Don't forget them.) Daniela grabs them. Her mother also hands her a sandwich. "¿Me lo preparaste?" (You made it for me?) "Sí, te lo preparé anoche." (Yes, I made it for you last night.) Two tiny words, te and lo, carry a whole sentence of meaning: for you, it.

At the bus stop she checks her bag. The calculator is not there. She texts her brother: "¿Viste mi calculadora?" (Did you see my calculator?) He answers: "La tienes en la mochila, bolsillo de adelante." (You have it in the backpack, front pocket.) She looks. There it is. She did not have to write calculadora again; la did the job.

On the bus, Daniela and her friend Tomás quiz each other. "Nos ayudamos siempre," (We always help each other) Tomás says. By 7:55 she is in her seat, notes read, calculator found, sandwich half eaten. Nothing about the morning went the way she planned, and yet every small word landed exactly where it belonged.
story.think: Daniela's morning is full of tiny words: me, te, lo, la, los, nos. Which of them mean the person doing the action, and which mean someone or something else?

lessons.title: Finding the Direct Object
lessons.mainIdea: The direct object receives the action, and Spanish replaces it with lo, la, los or las.
reading: Tomás texts his sister: "¿Tienes la calculadora?" (Do you have the calculator?) She answers, "Sí, la tengo." (Yes, I have it.) The word la is standing in for la calculadora. It is a *pronombre de objeto directo* (direct object pronoun). The direct object is the noun that receives the action of the verb. Ask "what?" or "whom?" after the verb, and the answer is the direct object: I have what? The calculator.

Spanish has four third-person direct object pronouns, and they match the noun in gender and number: *lo* (him, it, masculine), *la* (her, it, feminine), *los* (them, masculine or mixed), *las* (them, feminine). "¿Compraste los boletos?" (Did you buy the tickets?) "Sí, los compré." (Yes, I bought them.) "¿Conoces a Marta?" (Do you know Marta?) "Sí, la conozco." (Yes, I know her.) People and things use the same pronouns.

The pronouns for me, you and us are easy because they never change for gender: me (me), te (you, familiar), nos (us). "Mi mamá me despierta." (My mom wakes me.) "Te llamo mañana." (I'll call you tomorrow.) "El profesor nos escucha." (The teacher listens to us.) The common English-speaker mistake is to translate it as lo every time. If the noun is feminine, it is la: la tarea (the homework) → la hago (I do it).

words.d: direct object pronoun — replaces the noun that receives the action: lo, la, los, las, me, te, nos
him or it (masculine) — Veo el libro → Lo veo (I see it)
her or it (feminine) — Veo la casa → La veo (I see it)
them — Veo los libros → Los veo; Veo las casas → Las veo
the calculator — a feminine noun, so it becomes la

look.title: Replace the Noun
look.text:
Read each sentence and find the direct object.
1. Daniela busca la calculadora. (Daniela looks for the calculator.)
2. Tomás lee los apuntes. (Tomás reads the notes.)
3. Mamá prepara el sándwich. (Mom makes the sandwich.)
4. Los estudiantes escuchan a la profesora. (The students listen to the teacher.)
Now say each one again with a pronoun: Daniela la busca. Tomás los lee...
look.prompt: Finish sentences 3 and 4 with the right pronoun. What did you check to pick lo, la, los or las?

check.q: Which pronoun replaces la tarea in "Hago la tarea"?
check.why: Tarea is feminine singular, so the direct object pronoun is la.

check.q: What does "Los conozco" mean?
check.why: Los is the direct object pronoun for a masculine or mixed plural group: them.

check.q: Which sentence uses the pronoun correctly for "the tickets"?
check.why: Boletos is masculine plural, so the direct object pronoun is los.

lessons.title: Where the Pronoun Goes
lessons.mainIdea: A direct object pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb, and no before the pronoun.
reading: In English the pronoun follows the verb: I see it. In Spanish it comes first: Lo veo. The pronoun sits directly in front of the *verbo conjugado* (conjugated verb), the verb with a person ending. "Mi hermano me despierta." (My brother wakes me.) "¿La calculadora? La tengo." (The calculator? I have it.) Nothing squeezes between the pronoun and the verb.

When the sentence is negative, *no* goes before the pronoun, not between the pronoun and the verb. "No lo tengo." (I don't have it.) "No te escucho." (I can't hear you.) English speakers often write "Lo no tengo" because English puts the negative next to the verb. Remember the order: no + pronoun + verb.

In a question the order stays the same; only the intonation and the question marks change. "¿Me escuchas?" (Are you listening to me?) "¿Los viste?" (Did you see them?) Subject pronouns, when they appear, go before everything: "Yo no la conozco." (I don't know her.) Say the chain out loud a few times until it feels natural: yo no la conozco, tú no la conoces, ella no la conoce.

words.d: the conjugated verb — a verb with a person ending, like tengo or escuchas; the pronoun goes right before it
I don't have it — no comes before the pronoun, never between the pronoun and the verb
to listen — Te escucho (I'm listening to you)
to know a person or place — La conozco (I know her)

look.title: Fix the Word Order
look.text:
Each sentence has English word order. Rebuild it in Spanish order.
1. Tengo lo. (I have it.)
2. Lo no veo. (I don't see it.)
3. ¿Escuchas me? (Are you listening to me?)
4. Ella conoce no los. (She doesn't know them.)
The pattern: (subject) + no + pronoun + conjugated verb.
look.prompt: Rewrite all four. Which one was the hardest to hear as wrong, and why?

check.q: Which sentence has the correct order for "I don't have it"?
check.why: The order is no + pronoun + conjugated verb: No lo tengo.

check.q: Where does the pronoun go in "Are you listening to me?"
check.why: Me goes directly before the conjugated verb escuchas.

check.q: What does "Ella no los conoce" mean?
check.why: Los is them; ella is the subject, so she doesn't know them.

lessons.title: Attached to Infinitives and Gerunds
lessons.mainIdea: With an infinitive or a gerund the pronoun may attach to the end, and a gerund then needs a written accent.
reading: Daniela says, "Voy a leer los apuntes." (I'm going to read the notes.) With a pronoun she has two choices, and both are correct: "Los voy a leer" or "Voy a leerlos." The pronoun can go before the conjugated verb (voy) or attach to the end of the *infinitivo* (infinitive, the -ar, -er, -ir form). Attached, it is written as one word: leerlos, comprarla, verte.

The same two choices exist with the *gerundio* (gerund, the -ando / -iendo form) after estar. "Estoy leyendo los apuntes" becomes "Los estoy leyendo" or "Estoy leyéndolos." Notice the accent that appeared on leyéndolos. A gerund is stressed on the syllable before -ndo: le-YEN-do. Adding -los makes the word longer, so Spanish writes an accent to keep the stress where it was: leyéndolos, comiéndola, esperándote.

Infinitives usually do not need an accent when one pronoun attaches (leerlos, verte), because the stress already falls on the last syllable and one extra syllable does not break the rules. English speakers often forget the gerund accent, or add one to an infinitive where it does not belong. Rule of thumb: gerund + pronoun always takes an accent; infinitive + one pronoun does not.

words.d: the infinitive — the -ar, -er, -ir form; a pronoun can attach to its end: leerlos
the gerund — the -ando / -iendo form; with an attached pronoun it takes an accent: leyéndolos
reading them — gerund + pronoun, accent on the stressed syllable
to wait for — Te espero / Voy a esperarte (I'll wait for you)

look.title: Two Right Answers
look.text:
Write each sentence both ways.
1. Quiero comprar la calculadora. → La quiero comprar. / Quiero comprarla.
2. Estoy haciendo la tarea. → La estoy haciendo. / Estoy haciéndola.
3. Vamos a ver a los abuelos. → ?
4. Están escuchando la canción. → ?
look.prompt: Complete 3 and 4. Which of your four attached forms needed an accent, and why?

check.q: Which is a correct way to say "I'm reading them"?
check.why: The pronoun attaches to the gerund and the accent keeps the stress on -yén-.

check.q: Which sentence is NOT correct?
check.why: The pronoun goes before the conjugated verb or attached to the infinitive, never in the middle.

check.q: Why does comiéndola have an accent when comerla does not?
choices: Because the added syllable would move the stress off -mién-.
check.why: Adding a syllable to the gerund would shift the stress, so an accent marks the original stressed syllable.

lessons.title: To Whom and For Whom
lessons.mainIdea: The indirect object pronouns le and les mark the person who receives something, and Spanish usually adds them even when the noun is present.
reading: Daniela's mother made her a sandwich: "Le preparé un sándwich a Daniela." (I made a sandwich for Daniela.) The sandwich is the direct object, the thing made. Daniela is the *objeto indirecto* (indirect object), the person it was made for. Ask "to whom?" or "for whom?" after the verb, and you have found the indirect object.

The indirect object pronouns are me, te, le, nos, les. Only the third person differs from the direct ones: *le* (to him, to her, to you formal) and *les* (to them, to you all). They do not change for gender. "Le escribo a mi abuela." (I write to my grandmother.) "Les mando fotos a mis primos." (I send photos to my cousins.) "Te doy el libro." (I give you the book.)

Spanish often keeps both the pronoun and the noun in the same sentence: "Le preparé un sándwich a Daniela." This looks like a repeat to English speakers, but it is normal Spanish. The phrase *a Daniela* clears up who le means. Verbs of giving, telling and asking almost always take an indirect object: dar (to give), decir (to say), pedir (to ask for), mandar (to send), regalar (to give as a gift).

words.d: the indirect object — the person who receives, gets or is told something: to whom, for whom
to him, to her, to you (formal) — Le escribo (I write to him or her)
to them, to you all — Les mando fotos (I send them photos)
to give as a gift — Le regalo un libro a mi hermano (I give my brother a book)
to ask for — Te pido un favor (I ask you a favor)

look.title: Who Gets What?
look.text:
A: ¿Qué le regalas a tu mamá? (What are you giving your mom?)
B: Le regalo flores. ¿Y tú, qué les das a tus abuelos? (I'm giving her flowers. And you, what are you giving your grandparents?)
A: Les mando una tarjeta. (I'm sending them a card.)
In each line find the thing (direct object) and the person (indirect object).
look.prompt: Why does B say les and not le in the second question? What would change if the gift went to one grandfather only?

check.q: In "Le mando una foto a mi tía," what is le?
choices: The indirect object: to my aunt
check.why: Le marks the person who receives the photo, the indirect object.

check.q: Which pronoun fits: "___ escribo a mis padres."
check.why: Mis padres is plural, so the indirect object pronoun is les.

check.q: Which sentence means "I ask you for a favor"?
check.why: Te is the indirect object pronoun for you (familiar); pido is the yo form.

lessons.title: Two Pronouns Together
lessons.mainIdea: When a sentence has both pronouns, the indirect one comes first, and le or les becomes se before lo, la, los or las.
reading: "¿Me lo preparaste?" (Did you make it for me?) "Sí, te lo preparé." (Yes, I made it for you.) When both objects are pronouns, the indirect one comes first, then the direct one, and both go before the conjugated verb: me lo, te la, nos los. Think of the order as person first, thing second.

Now the twist. Spanish does not allow le lo or les la. When le or les comes right before lo, la, los or las, it changes to *se*. "Le doy el libro a Marta" becomes "Se lo doy." (I give it to her.) "Les mando las fotos a mis primos" becomes "Se las mando." (I send them to them.) This se is not reflexive; it is just le or les in disguise, changed so two l-words do not bump together.

Because se can mean to him, to her, to you (formal) or to them, Spanish often adds a clarifying phrase: "Se lo doy a ella" (I give it to her). Two English-speaker mistakes to watch for: writing le lo, and putting the direct pronoun first (lo se doy). The chain is always se + lo/la/los/las + verb.

words.d: to him, to her, to them — what le or les becomes before lo, la, los, las: Se lo doy (I give it to him)
it to me — indirect pronoun first, then direct: Me lo preparaste (You made it for me)
it (feminine) to you — Te la mando (I send it to you)
to give — doy, das, da, damos, dais, dan; Se lo doy (I give it to him)

look.title: Shrink the Sentence
look.text:
Replace both objects with pronouns.
1. Le doy la calculadora a Tomás. → Se la doy.
2. Te mando los apuntes. → Te los mando.
3. Les compro el regalo a mis padres. → ?
4. Nos explican la lección. → ?
5. Le pido las llaves a mi mamá. → ?
look.prompt: Finish 3, 4 and 5. In which ones did le or les change to se, and why?

check.q: Which sentence correctly replaces both objects in "Le doy el libro a Ana"?
check.why: Le becomes se before lo; the indirect pronoun goes first.

check.q: What does "Te la mando" mean?
check.why: Te is to you, la is it (feminine), mando is I send.

check.q: Why is there a se in "Se los di"?
choices: Because le or les changed to se before los.
check.why: Le or les always becomes se before a direct object pronoun beginning with l.

lessons.title: Double Pronouns on the End
lessons.mainIdea: Two pronouns can attach together to an infinitive or gerund, and the longer word always takes a written accent.
reading: Both pronouns can also attach to an infinitive or a gerund, in the same order, as one word: "Voy a dártelo." (I'm going to give it to you.) "Está explicándonoslo." (She is explaining it to us.) The pronouns never split up. Either both go before the conjugated verb (Te lo voy a dar) or both go on the end (Voy a dártelo).

When two pronouns attach, a written accent is always needed, even on an infinitive. Say dar-te-lo: the stress stays on dar, now three syllables from the end, so Spanish writes *dártelo*. The same goes for comprársela (to buy it for her), decírselo (to tell it to him), and any gerund: diciéndoselo, mandándotelas. Find the syllable that was stressed in the plain verb and put the accent there.

The famous example is the command *dámelo* (give it to me), which you will meet again in the next chapter. Da is the command, me is to me, lo is it. The stress stays on da, so the accent goes there. If you can build dámelo, cómpramela and explícanoslo, you have the whole system: verb + indirect + direct, one word, accent on the original stressed syllable.

words.d: to give it to you — infinitive + te + lo, with an accent because two pronouns attached
give it to me — the command da + me + lo, accent on da
to explain — Nos lo explica / Está explicándonoslo (She is explaining it to us)
the written accent mark — keeps the stress on the same syllable when pronouns make a word longer

look.title: Syllables Before and After
look.cite: Syllable counts of the verb forms in this lesson
look.prompt: The stress stays on the same syllable every time. Which forms in the table need a written accent, and what do they have in common?

check.q: Which is written correctly?
check.why: Two attached pronouns, indirect then direct, and an accent to keep the stress on dar.

check.q: What does "Está explicándonoslo" mean?
choices: He is explaining it to them.
He is explaining it to us.
We are explaining it to him.
check.why: Nos is to us, lo is it, and estar + gerund is an action in progress.

check.q: Which pair of sentences means the same thing?
choices: Te lo voy a decir. / Voy a decírtelo.
Te lo voy a decir. / Voy a decirlo te.
Lo te voy a decir. / Voy a decírtelo.
Te lo voy a decir. / Voy a decírselo.
check.why: Both pronouns go before the conjugated verb or both attach to the infinitive, in the same order.

lessons.title: Doing It to Yourself
lessons.mainIdea: A reflexive verb sends the action back to the subject, and its pronoun (me, te, se, nos, os, se) must match the subject.
reading: "Me ducho en tres minutos," Daniela says. Ducharse means to shower, to wash oneself. The subject (Daniela) and the object (Daniela) are the same person, so the verb is *reflexivo* (reflexive). In the dictionary a reflexive verb ends in -se: levantarse (to get up), ducharse (to shower), vestirse (to get dressed), acostarse (to go to bed).

To conjugate one, drop the -se, conjugate the verb as usual, and put the matching *pronombre reflexivo* (reflexive pronoun) in front: me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan. The pronoun and the ending must agree with the same subject. "Me levanto a las seis" (I get up at six), never "Me levanta."

Some of these verbs also have stem changes, which show in all forms except nosotros and vosotros: despertarse (e → ie): me despierto, te despiertas, se despierta, nos despertamos; acostarse (o → ue): me acuesto, nos acostamos; vestirse (e → i): me visto, nos vestimos. The pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb, just like the object pronouns you already know.

words.d: reflexive — the subject does the action to itself: Me lavo (I wash myself)
the reflexive pronoun — me, te, se, nos, os, se; it matches the subject
to get up — me levanto, te levantas, se levanta, nos levantamos, os levantáis, se levantan
to wake up — stem change e → ie: me despierto, nos despertamos
to go to bed — stem change o → ue: me acuesto, nos acostamos

look.title: Walk Through Ducharse
look.text:
ducharse → drop -se → duchar → conjugate → ducho, duchas, ducha, duchamos, ducháis, duchan → add the pronoun in front:
me ducho, te duchas, se ducha, nos duchamos, os ducháis, se duchan.
Now do the same with vestirse, remembering the e → i stem change in four of the six forms.
look.prompt: Write all six forms of vestirse. Which two forms keep the e of the stem, and why?

check.q: Which form is correct for "I get up"?
check.why: The reflexive pronoun me matches the yo ending -o: me levanto.

check.q: Which sentence has the right pronoun for nosotros?
check.why: Nos matches the nosotros ending -amos; nosotros has no stem change.

check.q: What does "Se despierta a las siete" mean?
choices: He or she wakes up at seven.
check.why: Se with the -a ending is the él/ella/usted form.

lessons.title: The Daily Routine
lessons.mainIdea: Spanish tells a routine with a chain of reflexive verbs and uses the definite article, not a possessive, for parts of the body and clothes.
reading: Here is Daniela's normal morning: "Me despierto a las seis, me levanto a las seis y cuarto, me ducho, me cepillo los dientes, me visto y me peino. Desayuno a las siete." (I wake up at six, get up at six fifteen, shower, brush my teeth, get dressed and comb my hair. I eat breakfast at seven.) Notice the last verb: desayunar is not reflexive, because breakfast is not done to yourself.

Look at *me cepillo los dientes* (I brush my teeth). English says "my teeth"; Spanish says "the teeth," because me already tells you whose they are. The same happens with clothes: me pongo la chaqueta (I put on my jacket), me quito los zapatos (I take off my shoes), me lavo la cara (I wash my face). Writing "mis dientes" is a common English-speaker habit; the article is the natural choice.

Some verbs change meaning when they become reflexive. Ir means to go; *irse* means to leave. Dormir means to sleep; dormirse means to fall asleep. Poner means to put; ponerse means to put on. Quedar means to remain; quedarse means to stay. "Me voy a las siete y cuarto" (I leave at seven fifteen) does not say where you are going, only that you are leaving.

words.d: to brush one's teeth — the article los, not mis, because me already shows whose
to put on (clothes) — Me pongo la chaqueta (I put on my jacket)
to take off (clothes) — Me quito los zapatos (I take off my shoes)
to leave — Me voy a las siete (I leave at seven); ir alone means to go
to fall asleep — Me duermo a las once (I fall asleep at eleven); dormir alone means to sleep
to eat breakfast — not reflexive: Desayuno a las siete

look.title: Daniela's Normal Morning
look.cite: Example schedule from the chapter story
look.prompt: Which verbs in the table are reflexive and which are not? On exam day she got up at 6:40; which steps did she probably skip?

check.q: Which is the natural way to say "I wash my face"?
check.why: The reflexive pronoun shows whose face it is, so Spanish uses the article la.

check.q: What does "Me voy" mean?
check.why: Irse, the reflexive form of ir, means to leave.

check.q: Which verb is NOT reflexive in a normal routine?
check.why: Desayunar (to eat breakfast) is not done to yourself, so it takes no reflexive pronoun.

lessons.title: Reflexive or Not?
lessons.mainIdea: The same verb is reflexive when the action stays with the subject and not reflexive when it goes to someone else.
reading: Daniela's brother wakes her up: "Mi hermano me despierta." On a normal day she wakes up by herself: "Me despierto a las seis." Both sentences have me, but they are different. In the first, me is a direct object: he wakes me. In the second, me is reflexive: I wake myself. The verb ending tells you which: despierta (he) versus despierto (I).

Many verbs work both ways. Lavar el carro (to wash the car) versus lavarse (to wash oneself). Acostar al bebé (to put the baby to bed) versus acostarse (to go to bed). Vestir a la niña (to dress the little girl) versus vestirse (to get dressed). The test: does the action land on the subject or on someone else? "La mamá viste a la niña" (the mom dresses the girl), but "La niña se viste" (the girl gets dressed).

The placement rules are the ones you already know. Before a conjugated verb: "Me quiero acostar." Attached to an infinitive: "Quiero acostarme." Attached to a gerund with an accent: "Estoy vistiéndome." The pronoun must still match the subject even when it is attached: "Vamos a levantarnos temprano" (we are going to get up early), not levantarse, because the subject is nosotros.

words.d: to wash something / to wash oneself — Lavo el carro; Me lavo las manos
to put someone to bed / to go to bed — Acuesto al bebé; Me acuesto a las diez
to dress someone / to get dressed — Viste a la niña; Se viste rápido
to get (ourselves) up — the attached pronoun still matches the subject nosotros

look.title: Same Verb, Two Directions
look.text:
1. Mi mamá despierta a mi hermano. (My mom wakes my brother.)
2. Mi hermano se despierta solo. (My brother wakes up on his own.)
3. Lavo los platos. (I wash the dishes.)
4. Me lavo las manos. (I wash my hands.)
5. Voy a acostar al perro. / Voy a acostarme.
In each pair, where does the action land?
look.prompt: Write one pair of your own with vestir / vestirse. What decides whether the pronoun appears?

check.q: Which sentence means "I put the baby to bed"?
check.why: The action goes to the baby, not back to the subject, so no reflexive pronoun is used.

check.q: Which attached pronoun is correct: "Vamos a ___ temprano"?
check.why: The subject is nosotros (vamos), so the reflexive pronoun must be nos.

check.q: In "Mi hermano me despierta," what is me?
check.why: The brother does the action to me; the subject and object are different people, so me is a direct object.

lessons.title: Each Other
lessons.mainIdea: With a plural subject, nos, os and se can mean each other, and context or el uno al otro makes it clear.
reading: On the bus Tomás says, "Nos ayudamos siempre" (we always help each other). The pronoun nos is *recíproco* (reciprocal): I help you and you help me. Reciprocal meaning only works with plural subjects, so the pronouns are nos, os and se. "Se escriben todos los días." (They write to each other every day.) "Nos vemos mañana." (We'll see each other tomorrow, a very common goodbye.)

Some of these sentences could also be reflexive. "Se miran" can mean they look at each other or they look at themselves. Usually the situation makes it obvious, but Spanish can add *el uno al otro* (each other) for reciprocal or a sí mismos (themselves) for reflexive. "Se ayudan el uno al otro." (They help each other.) "Se hablan a sí mismos." (They talk to themselves.)

Common reciprocal verbs: conocerse (to meet, to know each other), abrazarse (to hug each other), saludarse (to greet each other), quererse (to love each other), llamarse (to call each other), and verse (to see each other). "Mis abuelos se conocieron en Chicago en 1985" (My grandparents met in Chicago in 1985) is the kind of sentence you will hear in many families.

words.d: reciprocal — the action goes both ways: Nos ayudamos (we help each other)
each other — added to make the reciprocal meaning clear: Se ayudan el uno al otro
see you (we'll see each other) — a common way to say goodbye
to meet, to get to know each other — Se conocieron en Chicago (They met in Chicago)
to hug each other — Se abrazan al llegar (They hug when they arrive)

look.title: A Proverb with Te
look.text: Quien bien te quiere te hará llorar. (The one who truly loves you will make you cry.)
look.cite: Traditional Spanish proverb, origin unknown, in common use for centuries
look.prompt: Find the two pronouns te. Is either one reflexive or reciprocal? What kind of object is each?

check.q: What does "Nos escribimos cada semana" most likely mean?
choices: We write to ourselves each week.
They write to us each week.
We write to each other each week.
check.why: With a plural subject and a verb like escribir, nos is reciprocal: each other.

check.q: Which pronoun can NOT be reciprocal?
check.why: Reciprocal meaning needs a plural subject, so me (singular) cannot mean each other.

check.q: Which phrase makes "Se miran" clearly mean each other?
choices: Se miran el uno al otro.
check.why: El uno al otro means each other; a sí mismos would mean themselves.

review.why: Llaves is feminine plural, so the direct object pronoun is las.

review.q: Which sentence is in the correct order?
review.why: No goes before the pronoun, and the pronoun goes right before the conjugated verb.

review.q: Which form needs a written accent?
review.why: A gerund with an attached pronoun always takes an accent to keep its stress.

review.q: Which pronoun fills in: "___ regalo un libro a mi hermana."
review.why: Mi hermana is the person who receives the book, an indirect object: le.

review.q: How do you say "I give it (the book) to them" with two pronouns?
review.why: Les becomes se before lo; the book is singular, so lo.

review.q: Which sentence is correct for nosotros?
review.why: The reflexive pronoun nos matches the nosotros ending -amos.

review.q: What does "Se quita los zapatos" mean?
choices: He or she takes off his or her shoes.
review.why: Se with the -a ending is él/ella, and quitarse means to take off.

review.q: What does "Mis primos se llaman todos los días" mean?
choices: My cousins are named every day.
My cousins call each other every day.
My cousins call me every day.
My cousins call them every day.
review.why: With a plural subject, se is reciprocal here: each other.
